Photograph: Jess Hurd/PA Cotton Capital: ongoing series Reparations and reparative justice Jamaican delegation defends legal route of petition to King Charles for slavery reparations Petition to king, who remains Jamaica’s head of state, is formally lodged in landmark visit to UK by officials Natricia Duncan Caribbean correspondent Sat 12 Sep 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 07.01 EDT Share A palpable surge of emotion swept through Brixton’s New Park Road Baptist church as the packed congregation rose to sing Bob Marley’s Redemption Song. The service on Sunday marked the anniversary of the 1781 Zong massacre , when more than 100 enslaved Africans were thrown overboard so the ship’s owners could claim insurance for “lost cargo”. Jamaica’s plea to the king: use your authority to ensure colonial slavery is examined | Olivia Grange Read more And the song – a lament for the horrors of transatlantic slavery and a tribute to the resilience of those who fought for freedom – set the tone for a landmark visit to the UK by Jamaican officials to petition King Charles over reparations for slavery. The petition, backed by leaders of other Caribbean nations , asks the monarch to request legal advice from the privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries. It asks Charles, who is still Jamaica’s head of state, to seek guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences. Led by the culture minister, Olivia Grange , the Jamaican delegation included lawyers and members of the country’s national council on reparations. The delegation met diaspora communities, UK politicians, church leaders and institutions – including the British Museum, from which Jamaica is seeking the return of artefacts. Grange also held talks with the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, though sources say these were not focused on reparations. View image in fullscreen Olivia Grange, Jamaica’s culture minister, took part in a service at a Brixton church during her delegation’s visit to London. Photograph: Alberto Pezzali/AP Jamaica’s petition has ignited a fierce debate about the legality of transatlantic slavery and political implications. The former privy council member Lord Sumption dismissed the legal strategy as “nonsense” and argued that the issue was “not a question of law at all” but one of morals and politics. Jamaican experts have defended the legality of the petition. Speaking at a briefing for UK parliamentarians, Edward Fitzgerald KC insisted Jamaica was acting in accordance with a little‑used mechanism in the Judicial Committee Act 1833 which allows the king to refer questions of “legal or constitutional nature” to the privy council when they cannot be resolved through ordinary courts. Harj Narulla, a member of the UK team of counsels, told the Guardian it was an “obvious jurisdictional route”. “It was quite clear you can’t do a judicial review, for example, of some government decision … The issue is with the state itself, with the United Kingdom, which is the state responsible for slavery in Jamaica,” he said. Ulele Burnham, another member of the UK legal team, added: “The petition argues that the atrocities, the forced uprooting, the violent subjugation for profit was of course immoral, everyone knows that. But the petition’s very focus is to show that it was also clearly inconsistent with the law of the time. Non-Europeans did not suddenly become human when slavery ended. They always were. And even in those days, humans had some rights in English and international law.” In Jamaica, though the pursuit of reparations is supported by the two main parties, members of the opposition People’s National party raised concerns that the delegation had not managed to secure a meeting with the king. Grange said a meeting with Charles “was not part of the plan”. “Before we came to London , we had consulted with both the Palace and the privy council to confirm the correct legal process for filing the petition. Both confirmed the correct process was to file it by post and email, which is what we did,” she said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Monthly Sign up to Cotton Capital Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill in London, said the Jamaicans were ‘enacting their rights under English law’. Photograph: Bell Ribeiro-Addy The Labour MP Bell Ribeiro‑Addy, the chair of the all‑party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations, said Jamaica was well within its rights to petition the monarch. “Due to colonialism, which obviously initially had its root in enslavement, there are certain responsibilities that [the UK] has. We don’t get the privilege of still having Jamaica as part of the realm … without them also in turn having the right to petition King Charles. They are enacting their rights under English law and they have the right to ask those questions,” she said. In December 2024, Jamaica’s government tabled a bill in parliament to remove the king as the country’s head of state . The bill has not progressed to becoming a law. Pointing to recent global momentum – including 123 nations voting for a UN resolution describing chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity – Ribeiro‑Addy said it was time for Britain to confront its past and the decisions that continue to shape the present. She described headlines quoting huge reparation figures (which were not mentioned in the Jamaican petition) as a distraction. “What seems to happen a lot when we talk about reparations is people want to distract people with figures,” she said. “They divorce themselves from the reality of what we are talking about. No one is saying that reparative justice will never include any sort of payment. But that is never the starting point. And we have to remember that this country refuses to even apologise. This country refuses to do the things that it can do, which don’t cost any money at all. “The enslavement of peoples of African descent … meant that anybody who was not white was considered less than … almost being classified as not quite human. And that is a serious issue. If we are ever going to challenge racism properly, we have to get down to its very root.” As the delegation lodged the petition on Monday, a spokesperson for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”. Ribeiro‑Addy said it would be an insult to African and Caribbean countries if Britain refuses to discuss reparations at the upcoming Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua, which the king is scheduled to attend. “We’re meant to no longer be a group of countries under an empire. We were meant to be a group of countries with a shared history and who are treated as equals,” she said. “The idea that all of the countries bar one want to have a discussion and so the discussion is stopped has to be wrong … if we do things like that, I think we will soon see the crumbling of the Commonwealth. And that would be a huge shame.” Explore more on these topics Reparations and reparative justice Cotton Capital: ongoing series Slavery Jamaica King Charles III Colonialism British Museum London news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee C of E’s £100m plan to address historical links to slavery faces legal challenge Macron says France must address issue of reparations for its role in slave trade UK stole 25m years of life and labour through slavery in Barbados, says report UK will not apologise for role in slavery at Commonwealth summit, No 10 says Reform UK would stop visas for people from countries seeking slavery reparations Anglican group launches £7m project in Barbados to atone for slavery atrocities Jamaican delegation to travel to UK to lodge formal slavery reparations petition with King Charles Caribbean leaders back Jamaica petition to King Charles for slavery reparations Rise of far right makes reparations debate tough, says Cape Verde president Most viewed Most viewed

BUCHAREST, Romania (AP) — Tens of thousands of people gathered in Romania ’s capital Saturday to sit down at a miles-long table to break a Guinness record and raise money for what organizers said will be the country's first pediatric psychiatry hospital. Log in here » BUCHAREST, Romania (AP) — Tens of thousands of people gathered in Romania ’s capital Saturday to sit down at a miles-long table to break a Guinness record and raise money for what organizers said will be the country’s first pediatric psychiatry hospital. The 5,055-meter (3.1-mile) “Uniting Table” was sprawled along Unirii Boulevard to Constitution Square in front of Bucharest’s massive communist-era Palace of Parliament. The Romania-based organizers Bloom The World Association were awarded a certificate by Guinness World Records for the “longest table made from recycled materials.” The event brought together a reported 20,000 people at the many tables, many of which were decorated with flowers and snacks. People sit at a 5-kilometer (3.1 miles) long "Uniting Table", made from recycled materials, during a Guinness World Record event to raise money for a children's psychiatric facility, outside the communist-era built Palace of Parliament, in Bucharest, Romania, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. (AP Photo/Andreea Alexandru) Joanne Brent, a senior adjudicator and official onscreen judge for Guinness World Records, who joined the Bucharest event, said on stage that it proved that the record-breaking achievement had been put to good use. “Everyone, 20,000 people I am told are here today, have come around one table and a common cause,” she said. “I get to see this often, people coming together, record-breaking achievements with real-world impact.” Money raised from the event will go toward a 3,900-square-meter children’s psychiatric facility within the Obregia Hospital complex in Bucharest. It is being funded by private donations and sponsorships and will cost an estimated 16.5 million euros, according to the Metropolis Foundation, which is behind the construction project. “It is a project that started from a real need,” the foundation states on its website. “The current section at Obregia Hospital operates in an old, overcrowded space, which no longer meets the medical and emotional needs of children. … It means the chance to bring closer to reality a hospital that will benefit over 5,700 children facing severe mental illnesses annually.” The foundation says the number of children diagnosed with serious mental disorders, such as depression, behavioral disorders, substance use, autism and ADHD, has “increased alarmingly” in Romania, from 3,839 in 2018 to more than 5,600 in 2024. The hospital’s current pediatric psychiatry clinic has 62 beds, but wards with many beds that lack their own bathrooms, according to the foundation. It also states that the old facility’s lack of space can make private discussions with patients and their families challenging. The new five-level building will host medical offices, occupational therapy and virtual reality rooms, sensory and educational spaces, dedicated relaxation spaces, as well as a section dedicated to treating addiction among adolescents. “We clearly want as many people as possible to donate (toward) the first psychiatric hospital for children,” said Alexa Vilcan of Bloom the World. Winnipeg Free Press | Newsletter Jen Zoratti | Next Wednesdays What's next in arts, life and pop culture. Sign up for Jen Zoratti | Next The previous Guinness record for the longest table made from recycled materials was also held by Bloom the World, measuring 2,782 meters in Romania’s central town of Alba Iulia, and was recorded on the same date last year. In 2023, Romania had one of the lowest healthcare budgets in the European Union relative to GDP at 5.7%, compared to a bloc average of about 10%, according to the EU’s statistics office, Eurostat. Romania’s Minister of Health Alexandru Rogobete has pledged to support the initiative by supplying the “equipment and furniture necessary” to equip the medical facility, construction for which is scheduled to be completed by 2027. ___ McGrath reported from Leamington Spa, England. https://www.dw.com/en/nord-stream-german.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OByz Massive quantities of methane gas bubbled on the surface of the Baltic Sea after the explosion of the Nord Stream pipelines Image: Danish Defence Command/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO Advertisement The aerial photos made headlines worldwide: On September 26, 2022, massive quantities of methane gas bubbled on the surface of the Baltic Sea near the island of Bornholm. Unknown people had blown up three of the four sections of the Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines from Russia to Germany. The attack, which occurred seven months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine , meant the end of a mega energy project between Germany and Russia in which both sides had invested billions, and which secured affordable Russian gas for Germany. However, the flow of gas via Nord Stream 1 had been restricted or stopped several times by Russia since the Ukraine war began; Nord Stream 2 was not yet operational. From October 14, Ukrainian citizen Serhii K. is facing trial before a court in the northern German city of Hamburg. He was arrested in Italy in August 2025 on a European arrest warrant and later extradited to Germany. This week he must answer for the attacks before the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court. He is accused of being an accomplice to a war crime by attacking civil energy infrastructure, disruption of public services, causing an explosion and destroying structures. 5 things you need to know about Nord Stream To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Ukraine aid criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly said that Ukraine was not involved in the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream underwater gas pipelines . "Ukraine has never officially taken part in any operation related to the blowing up of Nord Stream," Zelenskyy told reporters again in August in response to a question about the ongoing investigation. The fact that the accused is Ukrainian is especially politically sensitive. Germany continues to support the country after it was attacked by Russia: militarily, financially, with humanitarian aid and by taking in about 1.3 million refugees. Critics of Germany's support for Ukraine, especially the right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing populist Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Moscow, resume energy deliveries from Russia – including via a repaired Nord Stream pipeline — and stop supporting Ukraine. Some of them have practically delivered their verdict on Serhii K., although the trial has not yet begun, and assume that Ukraine's political or military leadership was behind the attack on the pipeline. Sahra Wagenknecht, former leader of the BSW, told news agency Reuters in 2025 following Serhii K.'s arrest: "It is totally absurd that Germany spends many billions on aid for Ukraine but never demands an explanation from [President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. Questions should also be raised about possible compensation." Alice Weidel , co-leader of the AfD, has shared similar sentiments. In early 2026, she asserted that the German government must seek financial repayment from Ukraine. If the AfD came into power, she would demand Kyiv compensate Germany for blowing up the pipeline and pay for its repair. According to her, a country that does such things is "no friend of Germany." She has, however, failed to provide proof that Ukraine was behind the attack. Who benefited from blowing up the pipeline? In an interview with public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk in 2023, German naval commander Göran Swistek pointed out that, given the technical, financial, and organizational effort involved, “there is likely a state-run structure behind it.” In his opinion, a group of amateurs could not have carried out the act. However, he considered it unlikely that this state could be Ukraine, since Ukraine, after all, would not want to jeopardize German support. At the time, Swistek thought a false lead pointing to Russia was possible. The German-Russian Nord Stream project had many opponents from the beginning, including Poland, the US, the Baltic countries and — especially since Russia's full-scale invasion — Ukraine. That is why investigators always ask: Who benefits from the explosion? Henning Hoff from the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) thinks it is important to shed light on the background context. "By halting supplies or using the threat to do so as leverage, Russia exerted immense pressure on Germany at the time, and gas markets went haywire," he told DW. "The explosion thwarted Russian attempts to extort Germany, prices for natural gas sank. I think one could say: The explosion was in German interests." Can Ukraine still count on Germany? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Berlin's dilemma But what will happen if the Ukrainian Serhii K. is found guilty and a connection to the military or political leadership of Ukraine is proven? Could the German government still continue its current course regarding Ukraine? The German government faces a dilemma: On one side, judicial independence must be preserved and consequences for the sabotaging German infrastructure must be pursued. On the other side, the German government wants to prevent Russia from instrumentalizing the case. However, pressure on Germany would increase enormously, also from within the country. Roderich Kiesewetter, a lawmaker with the ruling center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), said there is no reason to deviate from the current course of support, even in the case of involvement by Kyiv: "Irrespective of the outcome, no consequences at all are appropriate, because our support for Ukraine is carried out in the interest of our own national security and stems from a sense of responsibility for a free Europe." The debate around support for Ukraine is escalating in Germany, regardless of the court process. Public backing for Ukraine is decreasing, especially for deliveries of weapons. The AfD gained significant support in three state parliament elections held in eastern Germany during September. The party could potentially supply the state premier in Saxony-Anhalt . The AfD has also led nationwide polls for months, far ahead of the conservative CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz . In addition, the AfD and BSW have drawn a connection between planned government spending cuts on social services and aid to Ukraine. Wagenknech told a campaign event before the state parliament elections that the federal government was "Sinking billions upon billions into the black hole of Ukraine, while in Germany, in our schools, the children are no longer properly learning reading, writing and arithmetic." Tino Chrupalla , co-leader of the AfD, raised the question of whether citizens were prepared to spend so much money on a non-EU and non- NATO country. Germany's chemical industry hit by high energy prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Repair of Nord Stream unlikely Given very expensive energy costs, it is not only the AfD and BSW who suggest repairing Nord Stream and receiving new deliveries of gas from Russia. Some CDU politicians favor this too, such as Saxony state premier Michael Kretschmer. He views a repaired gas pipeline as a possible bargaining chip for talks with Russia. Kretschmer's position, however, contradicts the federal CDU party line and European Union sanctions policies. His party colleague Kiesewetter considers it dangerous: "Russia has always used energy as an instrument of geo-economic extortion. It would be extremely dumb if we were to again learn nothing from history and cling to a special path with Russia. That would fuel mistrust among our partners in Europe. I can only advise everyone, including people from the CDU, to keep their distance from such calls, because they are against German interests." Hoff from the DGAP also rejected positions like Kretschmer's. "That is an illusion. There is no returning to the time before Russia's war. The supposedly cheap Russian gas, which has cost Germany dearly, will never flow again, if only because Putin has no interest in it doing so. It serves only as an instrument of propaganda for polarizing German politics and weakening support for Ukraine." In any case, the outcome of the trial in Hamburg will undoubtedly influence the public debate about further support for Ukraine. This article was originally written in German.
